title: KV cache reuse / eviction / paging / memory BW investigation
content:
Status: working notes / perf investigation (draft)

Context / motivation:
- Customers are seeing occasional latency tail spikes for long-context chat workloads. Hypothesis: KV cache reuse pattern + eviction/paging interactions are causing extra device<->host transfers or pathological kernel shapes that increase per-token time.
- This doc captures profiling runs, metrics definitions, early observations, and next experiments. Goal is to produce actionable mitigations (eviction policy tweaks, paging thresholds, prefetch heuristics).

Key questions:
- What is the observed KV reuse rate per request and per customer-workload class?
- How often do we evict hot KV entries (i.e., entries that are reused within the same conversation)?
- Are page faults / host<->device transfers correlated with tail latency spikes?
- Is memory bandwidth a limiting factor for our runtime kernel shapes when cache hit-rate changes?

Environments / hardware used:
- A100-40GB (dedicated cluster: rt-prod-gpu-3) for GPU runs.
- c6i.8xlarge (AWS) for CPU-only runs / paging emulation.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@main (commit 73a4b2) + KV-cache LRU v2 (feature branch merged-to-main on 2025-09-22).
- Profiling tools: Nsight Systems sampling + NVTX ranges, CUPTI metrics (DRAM throughput), Linux perf for CPU hotspots, iostat/vmstat for host page activity.

Metrics / signals we collect (definitions):
- KV_reuse_rate: tokens_reused / total_tokens_sent (measured per request and averaged). Reuse measured as prefix tokens that hit in KV store (not recomputed).
- KV_eviction_rate: evictions_per_minute / active_cache_entries.
- KV_paged_to_host: bytes moved from device to host due to eviction or memory pressure (aggregated).
- Page_faults_host: minor/major page faults observed on host process.
- Memory_bandwidth_utilization: % of GPU DRAM BW used during forward passes (CUPTI DRAM throughput / device peak).
- Per-token_latency_p50/p95/p99 (end-to-end as well as kernel-only).

Baseline observations (synthetic workloads):
- Workload A (long-chat, avg seq_len=4096, reuse-heavy): KV_reuse_rate ~ 0.62, p95 per-token latency stable. Memory BW util ~ 38% of A100 peak during generate kernels. Eviction_rate low (~0.04 evictions/min per GPU).
- Workload B (many short restarts, avg seq_len=64, low reuse): KV_reuse_rate ~ 0.07, p95 per-token latency increases by ~18% vs baseline; observed host<->device transfers spike during bursts. DRAM throughput spikes to ~68% of peak for short intervals.

Hot-path profiling notes (A100):
- NVTX-annotated runs show long stalls in the memcopy kernels when cache miss rate increases. These memcopies are pinned-memoryHostPinned->device transfers triggered by our current eviction path (we batch evictions, then page out a contiguous chunk).
- CUPTI metrics show aggregated DRAM throughput correlates with miss rate; when reuse drops below ~0.2 we hit transient BW > 60% and the host PCIe path becomes saturated causing longer enqueue-to-start times.
- Kernel-level execution times for attention and matmul kernels remain similar; the added latency is dominated by transfer and memcpy synchronization overhead.

OS/host signals:
- On c6i runs with simulated paging, we observed non-negligible major page faults when the host-side resident set grew due to our paging buffer logic (we were using MADV_DONTNEED too aggressively).
- iostat shows higher write throughput when eviction batches align with checkpointing; correlated with increased p99.

Eviction policy behavior (current LRU v2):
- Works well for steady reuse patterns. But in bursty traffic with interleaved short requests, LRU mis-orders some entries that are about to be reused (temporal locality across requests but interleaved by other users).
- We observed ~12% of evicted entries are re-requested within 5 seconds (measured during mixed workload trace). These reuses account for ~35% of extra device-host traffic.

Preliminary hypotheses:
1) Eviction batching + synchronous page-outs introduce head-of-line blocking on the host/PCIe path when miss-rate increases.
2) LRU recency alone is not capturing cross-request conversational locality patterns; workload-aware pinning (per-conversation or per-route hot lists) could reduce churn.
3) Paging thresholds tuned for memory pressure can be relaxed with an adaptive prefetch to avoid repeated evict/prefetch thrashing.

Experiments run so far (short notes + results):
- Experiment 1: Reduce eviction batch size from 4MB -> 512KB. Result: reduced p95 by ~9% on mixed workload (burst starts), but increased CPU overhead managing more frequent smaller copies.
- Experiment 2: Add soft-pin for last-N tokens per conversation (N=1024). Result: reuse of pinned region increased KV_reuse_rate by ~0.12 for long-chat flows; global memory use rose by ~7%; tail latency improved for long-chat but slightly worse for extremely low-reuse synthetic flows.
- Experiment 3: Background async prefetch for entries likely to be reused (heuristic: if conversation active in last 10s and next token predicted length > 512). Result: reduced observed host<->device spikes; however prefetch increased average DRAM utilization by ~6% and must be gated.

Data artifacts / locations:
- Traces: gs://internal-benchmarks/kv-cache/traces/2025-10-10/mixed-workload-nsight.zip
- CUPTI CSVs: gs://internal-benchmarks/kv-cache/cupti/2025-10-12/
- Aggregated metrics table (CSV): gs://internal-benchmarks/kv-cache/agg/kv-cache-agg-2025-10-15.csv

Open questions / next experiments:
- Tune eviction policy to be 'LRU + conversation pinning + adaptive aging' and measure real traffic for 48h. Can we implement conversation-scoped TTLs cheaply?
- Explore using CUDA Unified Virtual Memory (UVM) for very large models to avoid explicit page-outs; measure PCIe thrash tradeoffs vs explicit host pinned transfers.
- Add fine-grained NVTX around eviction batching code paths and collect more Nsight traces on production repros.
- Evaluate impact of prefetch gating thresholds to avoid unnecessary BW increase; target is tail latency improvement without >5% avg BW increase.

Immediate action items (owners):
- (Priya) Instrument eviction path with NVTX ranges + counters for evicted_entry_age distribution (due: 2025-10-22).
- (Marcus) Run 48h canary on dedicated cluster with soft-pin N=1024 enabled for one tenant; collect end-to-end latency + CUPTI metrics (due: 2025-10-29).
- (Ava) Prototype conversation-scoped TTLs in branch kv-pin-ttl and prepare perf microbench (due: 2025-10-25).
- (Liam) Draft PR with smaller eviction batch option toggled by runtime flag + telemetry for batching overhead (in progress: PR #482).

Risks / tradeoffs noted:
- Increasing pinning reduces churn but increases resident memory footprint; may force us into higher instance sizes or higher eviction pressure for multi-tenant nodes.
- Async prefetch helps tails but consumes additional memory BW that could interfere with peak compute kernels. Need dynamic gating.

Notes to self / scratchpad:
- Check if our allocator is returning host memory to OS quickly (madvise patterns). Might avoid host-side major faults.
- Look at kernel queue depths on PCIe (are we saturating NVLink vs PCIe depending on infra?).
- Correlate JFR traces with Confluence design doc to propose final policy changes.

References / earlier work:
- previous doc: kv-cache-investigation-reuse-eviction-bw.json (shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime) — keep for cross-reference.
- design notes: KV cache TTL proposal (Confluence link above).

Conclusion (current):
- Primary tail source appears to be device<->host transfer patterns driven by eviction/prefetch behavior, amplified under low reuse and bursty traffic.
- Short-term mitigations (smaller eviction batches, per-conversation soft pin) reduce tails. Long-term: adaptive eviction + smarter prefetching / UVM exploration.

TODO / follow-ups:
- Merge PR for batch size flag + telemetry (Liam).
- Run full prod-like A/B with 2% traffic for 72h (post PR).
- Draft runbook entry for operator toggles for eviction/prefetch flags.
summary: Investigation notes for KV cache reuse, eviction, paging, and memory bandwidth. Contains metrics, profiling results, experiments run, hypotheses, and next steps.
